title: America Still Has the Upper Hand Over China
gist: Two authors of 'Command of Commerce' argue against the prevailing view that Beijing is winning the economic confrontation, conceding recent US defeats — the April 2025 rare-earth export restrictions that forced Washington to drop tariffs, and a May 2026 Beijing summit where the US missed even its minimal goals — while holding that America retains an enduring economic power advantage if it works with allies. Only the opening section is available; the argument itself sits behind the paywall.

insights.claim: In April 2025, after Washington levied heavy tariffs on China, Beijing responded with export restrictions on rare-earth minerals that led the Trump administration to back down — a demonstrated case of Chinese chokepoint leverage defeating US tariff escalation.
insights.speaker: Ben A. Vagle
insights.so_what: Establishes rare-earth export controls as Beijing's proven de-escalation lever; price recurrence risk into any US tariff round and into rare-earth/magnet supply names.
insights.quote: Beijing responded with export restrictions on rare-earth minerals that led the Trump administration to back down
insights.locator: By most accounts, China has the upper hand

insights.claim: The consensus position as of July 2026 is that China holds the upper hand in its growing economic confrontation with the United States — a consensus these authors set out to contest.
insights.speaker: Ben A. Vagle
insights.so_what: Identifies where the crowded view sits; the contrarian case is that US structural economic advantage is being underpriced.
insights.quote: By most accounts, China has the upper hand in its growing economic confrontation with the United States.
insights.locator: By most accounts, China has the upper hand

insights.claim: At the May 2026 Trump-Xi meeting in Beijing the American delegation fell short of even its very limited objectives, according to the authors.
insights.speaker: Ben A. Vagle
insights.so_what: Summit diplomacy is not a reliable de-escalation channel for US-China trade risk; do not fade tariff/export-control risk on headlines of leader meetings.
insights.quote: the American delegation fell short of even its very limited objectives
insights.locator: And in May 2026, when U.S. President Donald Trump

insights.claim: The single notable deliverable from the May 2026 Beijing summit was China's agreement to buy 200 Boeing aircraft, a sharp step down from the 500 Trump had sought.
insights.speaker: Ben A. Vagle
insights.so_what: Hard number for Boeing's China order book — 200 units booked versus a 500-unit ask, i.e. 300 units of upside that did not materialise.
insights.quote: Beijing’s agreement to buy 200 Boeing aircraft, but even that was a big step down from the 500 he
insights.locator: The most notable success Trump could point to

themes.theme: Allied leverage as the US advantage

insights.claim: The authors' stated condition for American victory in the economic confrontation with China is coalition action — 'Washington Can Win If It Works With Allies' — implying unilateral tariff strategies are the losing variant.
insights.speaker: Ben A. Vagle
insights.so_what: Watch whether US export-control and tariff policy is multilateralised; allied coordination is the swing variable for how binding Chinese chokepoints remain.
insights.quote: Washington Can Win If It Works With Allies
insights.locator: America Still Has the Upper Hand Over China

insights.claim: Ben A. Vagle of Stanford and Stephen G. Brooks of Dartmouth ground their case in their book 'Command of Commerce: America's Enduring Economic Power Advantage Over China', framing US power as control over commercial flows rather than production share.
insights.speaker: Ben A. Vagle
insights.so_what: A named analytical framework — 'command of commerce' — for judging which chokepoints (shipping, finance, insurance) actually bind versus which are rhetorical.
insights.locator: BEN A. VAGLE is a Knight-Hennessy scholar
